codes.sample: 607 US adults who use ChatGPT (version 3.5) at least once a month; web-based survey distributed via the Centiment panel, February–March 2023.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (version 3.5)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The AI measures were Trust (7 items), Intent to Use (3 items) and Actual Use (a single frequency item, 1=once a month to 4=almost every day). The paper mentions overreliance only in its discussion and does not measure it.
codes.note: This is a TAM-style trust/intention/use study analysed with PLS-SEM, and only HTMT ratios and path coefficients are reported. There is no measure of dependence or problematic use, and no eligible psychological correlates (e.g., depression, anxiety, loneliness) were measured.

codes.sample: None. This is a systematic literature review of 37 empirical studies (2023–2024) on GenAI pedagogical applications in higher education. It collected no primary data from participants.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, custom GPTs, RAG chatbots, image/video generators), described across the reviewed studies
codes.dependence_measures: None. Over-reliance on GenAI comes up only as a theme in the thematic synthesis ('Student AI Literacy and Dependency', p. 11). No quantitative dependence measure was given.
codes.note: Methods (p. 3): 'This study follows a systematic review approach... PRISMA guidelines were followed.' This is a qualitative thematic synthesis with no quantitative psychological correlates. It also excluded survey-based studies, so none of its included studies are likely to be relevant sources for this review.

codes.sample: 300 full-time allied health students (e.g., BS nursing, BS midwifery) at one higher education institution in Central Luzon, Philippines; aged 18-31, 74% female; convenience sample surveyed online, Dec 2025-Jan 2026.
codes.ai_system: GenAI / AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, automated literature synthesis tools)
codes.dependence_measures: None for AI. The only AI measure is the 30-item "use of AI tools" scale by Ventura & Lopez (2024), with two parts: "awareness of use of AI tools" and "extent of use on the AI tools". It measures frequency, purpose and integration of use, not dependence. The dependence-type measure in the study is nomophobia (NMP-Q), which is about smartphones, not AI.
codes.note: AI use (awareness/extent) correlated with nomophobia r = .333 (Table 2, p.4). However, the AI measure is use/awareness rather than dependence, so the report fails I1. The text says data were collected in the "second semester" but the Limitations say "first semester". The Statistical Analysis section names JAMOVI, while the abstract says SPSS.

codes.sample: No human participants. GPT-4 itself was given the Russian MSCEIT V2.0 (sections B, C, D, F, G, H) in three runs; the scores were scored against Russian human norms (N = 3827).
codes.ai_system: GPT-4 via ChatGPT (it is the object being tested, not a system that people use)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study measures GPT-4's own emotional intelligence scores. It has no self-report measure of human dependence on, addiction to, or problematic use of AI.
codes.note: This is a 'machine psychology' case study that tests GPT-4's emotional intelligence on the MSCEIT, with no human sample. No AI-dependence measure and no human psychological correlates were collected. E1 is the primary reason; the study could also be seen as out of scope (E3), because the AI is what is being studied rather than something people use.

codes.sample: 135 adult Prolific participants from English-speaking countries (mean age 40.54, SD 13.17; 59.3% men), randomly assigned to an AI chatbot interviewer (n=44), a human interviewer (n=40) or an unmoderated condition (n=51); data collected Jan–Feb 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI companions in general (attitudes toward AI as friend, confidant, romantic partner); GPT-4-based chatbot 'Amanda' used as interviewer
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study used six single Likert items written by the research team on attitudes toward AI companionship (e.g., 'AI Companion as a Friend', 'AI as Emotional Support', 'AI Companion as a Romantic Partner'), plus one honesty item and qualitative codes. Over-reliance/dependence is only mentioned in the introduction and discussion.
codes.possible_duplicate: The 'AI-as-a-researcher' results from the same interviews are reported in a separate manuscript (p. 6). That is the same sample, but it is not relevant here because neither report has a dependence measure.
codes.note: Mixed-methods study (content analysis plus Welch ANOVAs across interviewer conditions). The AI measures cover attitudes and openness toward AI companionship only, with no dependence, addiction, problematic-use or emotional-dependence scale. No eligible psychological correlates were measured (no loneliness, anxiety, depression, etc.). 'Isolation' appears only as a qualitative barrier code.

codes.sample: None. This is a perspective/opinion article with no empirical data and no participants.
codes.ai_system: Generative chatbots in higher education (e.g., ChatGPT), discussed only conceptually
codes.dependence_measures: None. Over-reliance on and dependence on chatbots are discussed only in prose (e.g., "students becoming dependent on chatbots can lead to a lack of engagement", citing Fryer et al., 2020). Nothing was measured.
codes.note: Article is labelled "TYPE Perspective" (p.1) and described as "This short article introduces the ethical concerns". It covers data privacy, algorithmic bias, self-efficacy, plagiarism and hallucinations conceptually. There are no data, measures or statistics, so this is excluded as E5 (design).

codes.sample: 120 fourth-year public-university students in Bangladesh: 100 took the survey and 20 were interviewed (mixed methods). A pilot with 30 students came first.
codes.ai_system: AI tools for English learning in general (e.g., Grammarly, Duolingo, Babbel, ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence or addiction scale. The ad hoc survey has only descriptive items such as "Students heavily rely on AI tools for English learning" (90%, M = 4.6, SD = 0.2). These ask about reliance or use, not explicitly about dependence, addiction or being unable to stop. The other items cover usefulness, ease of use and attitudes (TAM-like).
codes.note: Even if the "heavily rely" item counted as a dependence measure, none of the eligible correlates was measured. The only inferential analyses involve usefulness, ease of use, frequency and language improvement, so the report would fail on no_eligible_correlate anyway.

codes.sample: 342 undergraduates at Anhui University of Science and Technology, China (114 per condition; 228 in the two AI-assisted conditions); aged 18–24, M = 20.21; 207 female. Three-condition between-subjects experiment run March–April 2026.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (GPT-5.4), used in open multi-turn sessions on reasoning and information-evaluation tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Overreliance was behavioural only: behavioural reliance (share of final answers matching ChatGPT) and acceptance of incorrect AI advice. Perceived reliance was a 4-item self-report of AI influence per task (α = 0.88); the authors say it was "not treated as a validated trait measure of dependence." No dependence or addiction scale.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate, academic self-efficacy (5 items, α = 0.83), was a control variable that appears only as a multivariable covariate (Table 5). Table 4 has no eligible correlate. Even if perceived reliance counted as the exposure, the report would be E4: no zero-order correlation with self-efficacy is reported.

codes.sample: 40 Chinese design-major freshmen and sophomores (28 female, 12 male; M age = 19.28, SD = 0.67) (p. 5).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT-4o (LLM chatbot) used during a design problem-solving task
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study used a within-subject experiment with think-aloud coding of higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) and expert ratings of sketches (CAT). "Direct adoption" of AI ideas was coded from behaviour in the task, and "high-/low-impact" groups were formed from changes in sketch scores. Neither is a self-report measure of dependence, over-reliance or problematic use.
codes.note: Experimental study (n=40). Over-reliance is only discussed in the text. There is no self-report AI dependence measure; reliance appears only as task behaviour (direct adoption of AI ideas). No eligible psychological correlates were measured. Outcomes were HOTS frequencies, ENA and the originality/usefulness of sketches.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative literature review with no participants or primary data.
codes.ai_system: Chatbots and AI in education, in general
codes.dependence_measures: None. Over-reliance on and dependence on chatbots are discussed only in prose (pp. 2-3). No quantitative dependence measure was given.
codes.note: Page 1 labels it "Article type: Review Article". It is a narrative review of the literature on how chatbots affect self-efficacy, self-esteem, problem-solving and critical thinking. It has no empirical data, no dependence scale and no correlations. Over-reliance is mentioned only conceptually ("Excessive dependence on chatbots for decision-making..." p. 3).

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a systematic review of 14 empirical studies on ChatGPT in education (searches run 3–10 April 2023).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (education settings)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The review mentions that 'overuse of ChatGPT may negatively impact innovative capacities' (p.1) only as a narrative synthesis. It gives no quantitative dependence measure.
codes.note: Labelled 'Review' and described as 'a systematic review of 14 empirical studies' (p.1). It contains no primary data. None of the included primary studies (Table 4) appears to measure AI dependence alongside psychological correlates. S7 (Strzelecki) is a UTAUT2 acceptance study.

codes.sample: 94 senior social-science undergraduates at an Egyptian public university (93 analysed, minus 2 outliers). The groups were formed by course enrolment: ChatGPT treatment (Social Network Analysis course) vs control (Data Mining course).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (assigned use for three essay assignments over about one month)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The exposure is experimental assignment to use ChatGPT ("In the treatment group, students were asked to write the essays using ChatGPT", p. 2). No self-report scale or item on dependence, addiction, problematic use or over-reliance is given. Outcomes are behavioural: innovation (lemonade stand game), risk (bomb risk elicitation task) and effort (cells filled in on a strategy sheet).
codes.possible_duplicate: The retrieved text is the bioRxiv preprint (doi:10.1101/2024.04.03.588037, posted April 5, 2024). The record lists a 2026 publication in Seikei ronsō, which is probably the published version of the same study.
codes.note: This is a field experiment in which ChatGPT use is manipulated, not a measure of dependence. "Dependence on technology" appears only in the theory section (p. 3). None of the eligible correlates were measured either: outcomes are innovation, risk-taking and effort. Exclude under E1.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a conceptual/literature-review conference paper by a single author (Politecnico di Milano).
codes.ai_system: Recommendation algorithms in social media and gaming (e.g., TikTok, Facebook), not interactive conversational or generative AI
codes.dependence_measures: None. The paper discusses addiction to digital experiences only conceptually and uses no quantitative measure.
codes.note: Abstract (p.1): "It is based on a literature review on addiction to digital experiences..." The paper is a theoretical/design-perspective piece with no data. It is also arguably out of scope (E3), since the AI here is the recommender systems behind social media, not interactive chatbots.

codes.sample: 808 first- and second-year undergraduates in a digital literacy course at a large Asian university (matched pre/post surveys from 3,030 registered students), who used generative AI during a collaborative problem-based learning task.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity)
codes.dependence_measures: Reliance Behavior Scale (Hou et al., 2025), a self-report scale of how often students used AI in four ways: reflective, cautious, collaborative and thoughtless use. Only 'thoughtless use' comes close to over-reliance. The other three subtypes describe ways of using AI, not dependence.
codes.possible_duplicate: Probably the same project/sample as Hou, Zhu, Sudarshan, Lim & Ong (2025), 'Measuring Undergraduate Students' Reliance on Generative AI During Problem-Solving: Scale Development and Validation', Computers & Education, 105329.
codes.note: The only correlates are critical thinking disposition and critical thinking skills (Table 1, polychoric correlations). Neither is on the list of eligible correlates. E1 could also be argued, because the Reliance Behavior Scale measures types and frequency of use rather than dependence; only the thoughtless-use subscale is close to over-reliance. Check the 2025 scale paper for eligible correlates.

codes.sample: None. This is a systematic review of 38 studies (PRISMA; Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, 2022–2024). No primary data were collected.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / ChatGPT in education (reviewed literature)
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. Over-reliance and dependency are discussed only in narrative form, citing other studies (e.g., ref [28], Zhang et al. 2024, 'Do you have AI dependency?').
codes.note: Systematic review: 'This study systematically analyzes the impact of generative AI on these skills using the PRISMA ... framework' (p. 1). The included study ref [28] (Zhang, Zhao, Zhou & Kim 2024, IJETHE, academic self-efficacy, academic stress, problematic AI usage) may be eligible and should be screened on its own.

codes.sample: 130 third-year medical undergraduates at a medical college in Central China; 128 valid questionnaires (33 ChatGPT users, 95 controls).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT used for academic writing (systematic review assignment)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The AI measures were ChatGPT use (yes/no), prior use, how often students used technology day to day, and items on recognition, acceptance and attitude. "Over-reliance" appears only as the authors' speculation (e.g., "This suggests a potential for over-reliance on such tools"). It was never measured.
codes.note: Group comparison of ChatGPT users vs non-users on writing time, article quality and self-rated writing skill/confidence/satisfaction. There is no dependence/addiction scale, and none of the eligible psychological correlates was measured. The study measured only use and attitudes/acceptance, so it is excluded under E1.

codes.sample: Planned: 160 college students aged 18–35 at Heidelberg University, Germany. No data reported (protocol only).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (GPT-4) used as a writing assistant in an RCT
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only AI-related measures are frequency of ChatGPT use for writing tasks (one item) and behavioural intention to use ChatGPT (two items). Over-reliance is named as a concern but is never measured.
codes.possible_duplicate: A future results paper from trial NCT06511102 may report the data from this protocol, but it would also lack a dependence measure.
codes.note: This is a study protocol with no results (E5_design). It would also fail E1: the only AI measures are use frequency and intention. The planned survey includes one stress item and a writing self-efficacy scale, but these will be analysed as intervention outcomes, not as correlates of dependence.

codes.sample: Semester-5 Madrasah Ibtidaiyah Teacher Education students (class of 2021), UIN Saifuddin Zuhri Purwokerto, Indonesia; number of participants not reported (qualitative interviews, observation, FGD).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: None quantitative. Over-reliance and addiction to ChatGPT are discussed only qualitatively, based on interviews and observation.
codes.note: Methods p.237: "This study used a qualitative descriptive research method"; uses a phenomenology approach with in-depth interviews, observation, documentation and Miles & Huberman analysis. There is no quantitative dependence scale and no psychological correlate is measured.

codes.sample: Nine MSc Marketing students at King's College London volunteered and eight completed all phases (entry focus group, audio diaries over 4 weeks, exit focus group); May–June 2023.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and other generative AI tools (e.g., Midjourney) used for coursework
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study uses qualitative content and thematic analysis of 65 audio diary entries. Dependency is mentioned only in the discussion ("risks of dependency and cognitive offloading") and the research agenda. No quantitative measure of dependence was used.
codes.note: Qualitative/conceptual study ("naturalistic inquiry", "interval-contingent diary method", "directed content analysis guided by Bloom's Taxonomy"). There is no quantitative dependence scale, no psychological correlates and no statistics. Table 2 gives only descriptive use frequency per participant.

codes.sample: None. Narrative review with no participants. Data availability: "This study is a narrative review and did not generate, collect, or analyse any new datasets" (p. 12).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (discussed conceptually in the context of health policy)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Overreliance/overdependency on ChatGPT is discussed only conceptually (pp. 7-10); no quantitative measure is administered.
codes.possible_duplicate: None. It cites primary studies that may themselves be eligible: Zhang et al. 2024 (AI dependency, academic self-efficacy, academic stress; ref 4) and Bouzar et al. 2024 (ChatGPT reliance and academic writing self-efficacy; ref 112).
codes.note: Abstract: "this narrative review focused on the implications of trust and overreliance on ChatGPT and critical thinking" (p. 1). Theoretical/review paper, so excluded as E5_design. Check the cited Zhang et al. 2024 (ref 4) and Bouzar et al. 2024 (ref 112) separately for eligibility.

codes.sample: 117 university students (mean age 22.61, SD 3.39; 70% female; 55% undergraduates), all speaking English as a second language. They were randomly assigned to four groups: control (n=30), ChatGPT 4.0 (n=35), human expert (n=25) and checklist writing-analytics tools (n=27). Lab experiment run July–September 2023.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT 4.0, embedded in the study platform as a writing and revision assistant (AI group)
codes.dependence_measures: None. "Metacognitive laziness" (dependence on AI) was inferred only from SRL trace data and process mining. The limitations note a "lack of targeted and matured measures for assessing metacognitive laziness" (p. 20). The questionnaire measures were the IMI and knowledge and transfer tests.
codes.note: Randomised four-group experiment. Over-reliance on AI is only interpreted from behaviour, and no self-report dependence scale was used. No eligible correlates were measured; the IMI pressure/tension subscale is task-state tension, not an eligible correlate. Results are reported only as group comparisons.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative/exploratory literature review (PubMed search; 29 articles analysed). No participants.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT / large language models (discussed conceptually)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Over-dependence on ChatGPT' and 'ChatGPT addiction' come up only as conceptual concerns (p. 4–5); nothing is measured quantitatively.
codes.note: Labelled 'REVIEW ARTICLE' (p. 1). The ethics statement says: 'Not applicable as it is a review article.' (p. 6). The paper offers the authors' perspective on how ChatGPT affects cognitive domains. It has no primary quantitative data, no dependence scale and no psychological correlates.
